demo:
def greet(name):
    print("Hello,", name)

# "Perth" is the argument
greet("Perth")
note: The value is the argument; the name it arrives under inside the function is the [[parameter]].
short: The actual value you hand to a function when you call it.

demo:
def area(width, height):
    # width and height are the parameters
    return width * height

print(area(3, 4))
note: A parameter is a name waiting for a value; an [[argument]] is the value that turns up.
short: The name a function gives to a value it is handed, written in its def line.

demo:
def double(n):
    return n * 2

result = double(21)
print(result)
print(double(5) + 1)
note: Returning is not printing. A function that prints shows you something; a function that returns gives you something you can use.
short: Hands a value back to whoever called the function, and stops the function there.

demo:
def shows(n):
    print(n * 2)

value = shows(21)
print("the call was worth:", value)
note: A function that prints instead of returning gives the caller nothing: the call is worth None.
short: Writes something on the screen for a person to read.

demo:
def nothing():
    pass

print(nothing())
print(None is None)
note: A function with no return statement hands back None, which is why printing its result shows None.
short: Python's word for "no value at all".

demo:
prices = [3, 5]
prices.append(7)
print(prices)
note: Changing a mutable value changes it for every name pointing at it — see [[aliasing]].
short: Able to be changed after it is made. Lists, dictionaries and sets are mutable.

demo:
name = "perth"
upper = name.upper()
print(name)
print(upper)
note: Operations that look like changes build a new value instead and leave the old one alone.
short: Cannot be changed once made. Strings, numbers and tuples are immutable.

demo:
a = [1, 2]
b = a
b.append(3)
print(a)
print(a is b)
note: Assigning a list to a second name does not copy it. Use list(...) or a slice to get a copy.
short: Two names pointing at the same value, so a change through one shows through the other.

demo:
days = ["Mon", "Tue", "Wed"]
print(days[0])
print(days[-1])
print(len(days))
note: The last item is at index len(x) - 1, which is why len(x) itself is out of range.
short: The position of an item in a list or string, counting from 0.

demo:
word = "Fremantle"
print(word[0:4])
print(word[:3])
print(word[-3:])
note: The stop position is not included, so x[0:2] gives two items.
short: A piece of a list or string, written x[start:stop].

demo:
point = (3, 4)
x, y = point
print(x, y)
print(len(point))
note: Like a list but immutable, which makes it safe to use as a dictionary key.
short: A fixed sequence of values, written with round brackets: (1, 2).

note: Asking for a key that is not there raises KeyError; .get() returns None instead.
short: The thing you look something up by in a dictionary.

note: Looping over a dictionary gives you its keys, not its values.
short: To go through something one item at a time, which is what a for loop does.

demo:
total = 0
for n in [2, 4, 6]:
    total = total + n
print(total)
note: It has to be created before the loop starts, or the first pass has nothing to add to.
short: A variable you set up before a loop and add to inside it.

demo:
print(2 + 2)
print("ab" * 3)
print(5 > 3)
short: A piece of code that produces a value: 2 + 2, name.upper(), x > 3.

note: An expression produces a value; a statement does something.
short: A complete instruction: an assignment, an if, a loop, a return.

demo:
print(3 > 5)
print(bool(0), bool(""), bool([]))
print(bool("no"), bool([0]))
note: Python also treats 0, "" and [] as false when it needs a yes or no, which is what "falsy" means.
short: A value that is either True or False.

demo:
print(0.1 + 0.2)
print(7 / 2)
print(round(2.675, 2))
note: Floats are stored in binary, so some sums come out a hair off: 0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3.
short: A number with a decimal point, like 3.5.

demo:
print(7 / 2)
print(7 // 2)
print(-7 // 2)
note: Dividing with / always gives a float; // keeps it whole and rounds down.
short: A whole number, with no decimal point.

demo:
first = "Swan"
print(first + " River")
print(first + str(2))
note: Both sides have to be strings: adding a number raises TypeError unless you convert it first.
short: To join two strings end to end with +.

demo:
name = "  perth  "
print(name.strip().title())
print("a,b".split(","))
note: A method acts on the thing before the dot, which is why it needs no argument for it.
short: A function that belongs to a value, called with a dot: name.upper().
A named block of code you can run whenever you want, by calling it.

demo:
def f():
    inside = 1
    print("inside sees:", inside)

f()
print("outside sees:", "inside" in dir())
note: That is why a variable made in a function vanishes when the function ends.
short: Where a name can be seen. A name made inside a function is only visible inside it.

note: Read it from the bottom: the last line names the error, and the line above it is usually your code.
short: The report Python prints when something goes wrong, listing where it happened.

note: try/except lets you catch one and decide what to do instead of stopping.
short: Python's way of stopping when it cannot carry on, like dividing by zero.

note: A SyntaxError means Python could not read the code at all, so nothing ran — not even the lines above it.
short: The grammar of the language: where the colons, brackets and indents go.

note: Four spaces per level is the convention. Mixing tabs and spaces is a common cause of errors.
short: The spaces at the start of a line, which is how Python knows what is inside what.

note: Without one the calls never stop, and Python gives up with RecursionError.
short: The case a recursive function answers directly, without calling itself again.

note: Every recursive function needs a [[base-case]] or it never stops.
short: A function that calls itself on a smaller version of the same problem.

note: A project brief that fixes a signature means calling it that exact way, with that many parameters.
short: The def line of a function: its name and the parameters it takes.
A value written directly in the code: 42, "hello", [1, 2].
A value an operator works on. In 2 + 3, the operands are 2 and 3.

note: A nested loop runs its whole inner loop for every single pass of the outer one.
short: One thing inside another: a loop inside a loop, or a list inside a list.

note: Everything else in markets is priced relative to it: a future is spot plus carry, an option is worth something only relative to it.
short: The price something trades at right now, for delivery now.

demo:
import math
old, new = 100, 110
print(round((new - old) / old, 4))
print(round(math.log(new / old), 4))
up = math.log(110 / 100)
down = math.log(100 / 110)
print(round(up + down, 10))
note: Log returns add up across days where percentage returns do not: up 10% then down 10% is not back where you started, but two log returns of +x and −x are.
short: The change in a price measured as the natural log of new over old, instead of as a percentage.

demo:
prices = [10, 12, 11, 13, 15, 14]
n = 3
for i in range(n - 1, len(prices)):
    window = prices[i - n + 1:i + 1]
    print(i, round(sum(window) / n, 2))
note: A longer window smooths more and lags more. The choice of N is a choice about how much you want to be told about what just happened.
short: The average of the last N prices, recomputed each day as the window slides forward.

note: High volatility is not "going down"; it is going anywhere fast. It is the one number that makes an option worth more the higher it is.
short: How much a price tends to move, measured as the standard deviation of its returns.

demo:
prices = [100, 120, 90, 110, 80]
peak = prices[0]
for p in prices:
    peak = max(peak, p)
    print(p, "drawdown", round((peak - p) / peak, 2))
note: A 50% drawdown needs a 100% rise to recover, which is why the size of the fall matters more than it looks.
short: How far a price has fallen from its highest point so far.

note: Its shape says what the market thinks holding the thing costs: upward is [[contango]], downward is [[backwardation]].
short: The prices agreed today for delivery at each future date, drawn as a line across those dates.

note: The normal shape for anything that costs money to store, because the seller must be paid for storing it until you want it.
short: A forward curve that rises with time: delivery later costs more than delivery now.

note: The market's way of saying it wants the thing now, not later — a sign of scarcity today.
short: A forward curve that falls with time: delivery now costs more than delivery later.

demo:
spot = 100
rate = 0.05
storage = 0.02
for years in [0.5, 1, 2]:
    fair = spot * (1 + rate + storage) ** years
    print(years, round(fair, 2))
note: Carry is the whole difference between spot and a fair futures price. Positive carry gives contango, negative carry gives backwardation.
short: What it costs to hold something from now until a future date: interest on the money tied up, plus storage, minus anything it pays you meanwhile.

note: It shrinks to zero as delivery approaches, because on delivery day a future and the thing itself are the same thing.
short: The gap between the spot price and a futures price for the same thing.

note: It is not the price of the future — you never pay that until delivery — which is what makes a future so heavily levered.
short: The deposit you must keep with the exchange while you hold a future, so that a loss can be taken from it.

demo:
account = 1000
prices = [100, 103, 101, 106]
contracts = 10
for i in range(1, len(prices)):
    account += (prices[i] - prices[i - 1]) * contracts
    print("day", i, "account", account)
note: A future never builds up an unpaid gain or loss the way a bet would. Each day is closed out and the next starts from today's price.
short: Settling a future's gain or loss every single day, moving cash into or out of the margin account.

note: Nothing about the market changes it. It is written into the contract on day one and is where the payoff bends.
short: The fixed price an option lets you buy or sell at.

note: For the buyer it is the most that can be lost. For the seller it is the most that can be made.
short: What an option costs to buy — the fee for the right it gives you.

note: Worth something at expiry only when the market is above the strike: max(spot − strike, 0).
short: An option that gives you the right to buy at the strike.

note: Worth something at expiry only when the market is below the strike: max(strike − spot, 0). Insurance on something you own.
short: An option that gives you the right to sell at the strike.

note: For a bought call it is the strike plus the premium; for a bought put, the strike minus the premium.
short: The spot price at which an option position has made back exactly what it cost.

note: An out-of-the-money option is not worthless before expiry — it is worth whatever chance it has of ending up in.
short: Where the spot is relative to the strike: in the money if the option would pay now, out if it would not, at if they are equal.

note: It speeds up near the end: the last week costs more of the value than the first month did.
short: The way an option loses value as expiry approaches with nothing else changing.

note: It is the market's opinion of how much the price will move, read backwards from what people are paying.
short: The volatility you would have to assume for a pricing model to give the option its market price.
